name: Kingdom of Colchis
info: The Georgian polity of Egrisi on the eastern Black Sea, known to the Greeks as Colchis, land of Medea and the Golden Fleece, rich in gold, iron, timber and honey, and reckoned the earliest Georgian state.

facts.capital: No single seat is recorded; the chief towns were Phasis (Poti), Dioscurias (Sukhumi), Surium (Vani), Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi) and Cyta or Aia (Kutaisi)
facts.predecessor: The Colchian Bronze Age culture of the eastern Black Sea; the Qulḫa of the Urartian inscriptions
facts.successor: Pontus under Mithridates VI, who gave Colchis to his son in 83 BCE; then Roman dynasts and the kingdom of Lazica (Egrisi)

sections.foundation:
Colchis was the Greek name for the Georgian polity of Egrisi on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in what is now western Georgia with Abkhazia and the neighbouring coasts of Russia and Turkey. Its people, the Colchians, are generally believed to have been early Zan-speaking tribes, ancestors of the Laz and Mingrelians, and Cyril Toumanoff called Colchis 'not a proto-Georgian, but a Georgian (West Georgian) kingdom', the earliest Georgian formation. The land is a humid plain between the Greater and Lesser Caucasus, closed on the east by the Likhi Range, where temperate rainforest once covered the lowlands. A Bronze Age Colchian culture, related to the Koban culture, grew up there, and by the end of the second millennium BCE urbanisation was well advanced in parts of the country; the Late Bronze Age brought skill in smelting and casting metals and sophisticated farming implements.

The name is thought to derive from the Urartian Qulḫa. Giorgi Melikishvili and Donald Rayfield read Colchis into Assyrian inscriptions: Tukulti-Ninurta I (1243–1207 BCE) defeated forty kings of Nairi and of 'the countries on the shores of the Upper Sea', and Tiglath-Pileser I (1114–1076 BCE) called himself conqueror of Nairi 'from Gilḫi to the Upper Sea', Gilḫi being read as Kilḫi, Colchis. In the mid-8th century BCE Sarduri II of Urartu inscribed a victory over Qulḫa, whose exact location is disputed.
sections.socioeconomy:
Greek writers described Colchis as a land rich in gold, iron, timber and honey, exporting its resources mostly to the Hellenic city-states, and in myth as a fabulously wealthy country on the periphery of the heroic world. Millet was the staple crop; wheat grew in some regions and was also imported by sea, and local wines were drunk alongside wines brought from overseas. The Colchian plain gave ample grazing for cattle and horses, the name of Phasis being associated with fine horses, and its wetlands held waterfowl: Colchian pheasants were exported to Rome, where moralists condemned them as a symbol of excess. Colchis provided slaves as tribute to the Achaemenid Empire, and Colchian slaves are attested in ancient Greece.

The country's towns lay along the shore and the rivers: Dioscurias, later the Roman Sebastopolis and now Sukhumi, Phasis at the mouth of the river of that name, the Rioni, Pityus (Pitsunda), Apsaros (Gonio), Sarapana (Shorapani), Surium (Vani), Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi) and Cyta or Aia (Kutaisi), the traditional birthplace of Medea. The population was diverse: Greek and Roman sources say that between 70 and 300 languages were spoken in Dioscurias alone. The influence of the Achaemenid Empire, with its thriving commerce and wide economic ties, accelerated the socio-economic development of the Colchian land. Greek was widespread, and decrees were even issued in that language.
sections.military:
Colchis fought its wars against the great powers to the south and the horsemen from the north. The polity of Kilkhi or Qulḫa warred first against the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser I and then against Urartu under Argishti I and Menua, and Sarduri II of Urartu claimed a victory over it in the mid-8th century BCE. From that century Scythians and Cimmerians migrating from Central Asia into the Pontic steppes invaded Colchis, and the Scythians made a base on the former territory of the kingdom from which they raided and campaigned in Media and Anatolia; Askold Ivanchik judges that Qulḫa, an independent flourishing state in the second half of the 8th century BCE, hardly survived the century's end.

Under the Achaemenids the southern tribes, the Macrones, Moschi and Marres, were incorporated into the 19th satrapy, while the northern tribes submitted 'voluntarily' and sent the Persian court 100 girls and 100 boys every five years. In 400 BCE, shortly after the Ten Thousand reached Trapezus, the Colchians fought them and were decisively defeated. Later the Colchians appear to have thrown off Achaemenid authority and formed an independent state. Mithridates VI of Pontus quelled an uprising in the region in 83 BCE, and Pompey occupied Colchis after Mithridates' defeat in 65 BCE, capturing the local chief Olthaces.
sections.governance:
Little is known of the rulers of Colchis. Pliny says the Colchians were governed by their own kings in the earliest ages, and the Greeks knew the mythical Aeëtes, son of Helios and father of Medea, with his city Aea or Aia, before Aeschylus and Pindar first used Kolchis for a region. After the Achaemenid period the Colchians formed an independent state that, according to Ronald Suny, was federated to Kartli-Iberia in the east; its kings ruled through skeptoukhoi, royal governors who received a staff from the king, and by David Braund's reading of Strabo the native dynasty continued to rule despite the country's fragmentation into skeptoukhies. The oldest 'Colchian' coins, from the mid-6th century BCE, long served as the primary evidence for a Colchian state, but reassessment shows them to be the production of an Achaemenid satrapy.

Classical sources bordered Colchis with Pontus to the south-west, the Black Sea to the west, the Greater Caucasus and Sarmatia to the north, Iberia to the east and Armenia to the south. In 83 BCE Mithridates VI gave the country to his son Mithridates, who was executed on suspicion of plotting against him. Pompey installed Aristarchus as dynast (63–47 BCE); under Polemon I, Pythodorida of Pontus and Polemon II Colchis belonged to Pontus until Nero induced Polemon to abdicate and the land was absorbed into the province of Galatia in 63 and Cappadocia in 81.
sections.impact:
Colchis is reckoned in modern scholarship 'the earliest Georgian formation', which with the Kingdom of Iberia contributed to the Kingdom of Georgia and the Georgian nation; Ronald Grigor Suny stresses the Colchians' part in the ethnogenesis of the Georgians, and Svante Cornell dates proto-Georgian statehood to the kingdom of Colchis in the 6th century BCE. The name Colchians became the Greco-Roman collective term for the early Kartvelian tribes of the eastern Black Sea coast, and in a later era it was joined to the name Lazi: by the 1st century BCE the kingdom of Lazica had formed in the region, known as Egrisi when it became a Roman vassal in 66 BCE after Pompey's campaign.

To the Greeks Colchis was Aea, from the 5th century BCE onwards the home of Aeëtes, Medea and the Golden Fleece, the goal of Jason and the Argonauts; here Prometheus was chained to a mountain for revealing fire to humanity, and here some placed the homeland of the Amazons. Herodotus, who is thought never to have gone there, imagined the Colchians dark-skinned and woolly-haired, called them Egyptians and said they practised circumcision as descendants of the army of Pharaoh Sesostris, claims modern historians have widely rejected. Christianity, by traditional accounts, was first preached in Colchis by Andrew the Apostle, Simon the Zealot and Matthias; a change in burial patterns in the 3rd century may show its influence.
sections.decline:
The Colchian state did not fall at once; it was absorbed. After it threw off Achaemenid authority it ruled through its skeptoukhoi, but in 83 BCE Mithridates VI of Pontus quelled an uprising in the region and gave Colchis to his son Mithridates, soon executed on suspicion of plotting against his father. On Mithridates' defeat in 65 BCE Pompey occupied the country, captured the chief Olthaces and installed Aristarchus as dynast from 63 to 47 BCE. Under Polemon I Colchis was part of Pontus and the Bosporan Kingdom; his widow Pythodorida kept it, and her son Polemon II was induced by Nero to abdicate, after which Pontus and Colchis were incorporated into the province of Galatia in 63 and Cappadocia in 81.

Phasis, Dioscurias and the other Greek settlements of the coast never fully recovered from the wars of 60–40 BCE, and Trebizond became the economic and political centre of the region. Roman rule was relatively loose: the Romans held the sea forts, mountain tribes such as the Svaneti and Heniochi raided the lowlands and ran their own kingdoms with nominal homage, and the uprising of 69 under Anicetus failed. Arrian, sent by Hadrian, found the Laz in control of most of coastal Colchis. Out of this the kingdom of Lazica, or Egrisi, emerged, the heir of Colchis in the Georgian tradition, while the name Colchis lived on in Greek and Roman geography and in the legend of Medea.

summary: Colchis, the Georgian Egrisi on the eastern Black Sea, was known to Urartu as Qulḫa and to the Greeks as the land of the Golden Fleece; a state in the 8th century BCE and again from the 6th, tributary to Persia, it ruled through royal governors until Pontus and then Rome absorbed it in the 1st century BCE.

notes: The article dates Colchis c. 13th to 1st centuries BC and gives no event at the register's end -101; the nearest dated events are the Ten Thousand (400 BC) and Mithridates VI's intervention (83 BC), the latter told in decline as what followed.

The points at -500 (Achaemenid satrapy and tribute) and -300 (independence under skeptoukhoi) are undated in the article and placed approximately; -730 reads 'second half of the 8th century BC', -750 'mid-eighth century', -550 'middle of the 6th century'.
The register's capital is Vani; the article names Surium (now Vani) among the chief towns but gives no capital, so the capital fact lists the chief towns.
The Urartian and Assyrian identifications (Qulḫa, Kilḫi) are given as the readings of the scholars the article names (Melikishvili, Rayfield, Gordeziani, Ivanchik), not as settled.
